cards.front: The CRR sets a hard PD input floor below which no estimated PD may fall for capital. For a retail-pooled Sektorrating grade, what is that floor (as a fraction)?
cards.sourceNote: 0.03% is set by CRR Art.163(1) for retail (Art.160(1) for corporate/institution). The module flags CRR III (from 2025) as having revisited IRB input floors; treat 0.03% as a live figure under the current regime.

cards.front: A single defaulted facility has \(EAD=\text{€}500{,}000\). Net recoveries discounted to the default date at the prescribed risk-free + 5% rate (here 8%) sum to €343,644. Give the realised LGD.

The loss-case LGD is 31.27%. Across the default-weighted pool 30% of defaults cure (and stay cured past the cure period) with \(\text{LGD}_{\text{cure}}=5\%\). Give the default-weighted pool LGD \((1-\pi_{\text{cure}})\,\text{LGD}_{\text{loss}}+\pi_{\text{cure}}\,\text{LGD}_{\text{cure}}\).

The long-run default-weighted pool LGD is 23.39%. Three non-overlapping MoC add-ons apply: A = +1.5pp (data/method), B = +0.8pp (relevant change), C = +1.2pp (residual estimation error). Give the final regulatory LGD before any downturn loading (as a fraction).

Calibrate a retail PD to its long-run central tendency and floor a tail grade. Year-by-year observed default rates over the 5-year window are 0.90%, 2.48%, 1.51%, 1.03%, 0.89%; the scorecard's raw exposure-weighted average PD is \(p^{\text{raw}}=1.10\%\).

steps.prompt: Compute the year-weighted (arithmetic) central tendency \(\overline{CT}\) of the five annual default rates.
steps.explain: (0.90+2.48+1.51+1.03+0.89)/5 = 6.81/5 = 1.362%. The year-weighted mean gives the crisis year (2020) equal standing — the prudent, central-tendency-faithful choice.

steps.prompt: Solve the one-parameter scaling \(\kappa=\overline{CT}/p^{\text{raw}}\) that lifts the portfolio-average PD to the central tendency.
steps.explain: 1.362%/1.10% = 1.238. Multiplicative scaling is monotone, so it fixes the level while preserving rank-ordering.

steps.prompt: A grade with raw PD 0.02% is scaled by κ then floored. What is its final PD?
steps.explain: 0.02%×1.238 = 0.0248% < the retail floor of 0.03% (CRR Art.163(1)), so it is lifted to 0.03%. Calibration fixes the level; the floor catches the tail.

cards.front: EBA/GL/2017/16 forbids discounting workout recoveries at the facility's effective interest rate. Instead, each net cash flow is discounted to the {{c1}} date using a {{c2}} rate.

Prescribed (not estimated) parameters: residential-mortgage retail correlation \(\rho=\) {{c1}}, QRRE correlation \(\rho=\) {{c2}}, and the maturity adjustment \(b(\mathrm{PD})=(0.11852-{{c3}}\cdot\ln \mathrm{PD})^2\).
Under Foundation-IRB the bank self-estimates PD but takes fixed inputs: senior-unsecured LGD = {{c1}}, subordinated LGD = {{c2}}, and effective maturity \(M\) defaults to {{c3}} years.
cards.sourceNote: Module notes the F-IRB 45%/75% LGDs are themselves subject to CRR III change; confirm for the current regime.

cards.front: An inspector finds your missing-downturn correction to the long-run average has been folded into the Category-C Margin of Conservatism. Distinguish the appropriate adjustment from the MoC and state the error.
rubric: The appropriate adjustment (CRR Art.181(1)(b)) corrects a KNOWN structural gap in the long-run average — e.g. a missing bad year in an unrepresentative observation period.
The MoC adds a cushion for RESIDUAL uncertainty on top of an already best-estimated parameter (categories A data/method, B relevant change, C statistical error).
Both are CRR/EBA-mandated regulatory instruments — neither is an ÖRS proportionality choice.
Folding the missing-downturn correction into Category-C MoC (or vice versa) is a methodological error, and if both are present it is a double-count — a fast TRIM-inspection failure.

cards.front: A colleague cites CRR Art.160(1) to floor a retail-pooled Sektorrating PD at 0.03%. Is the citation and the floor itself a regulatory value or an ÖRS choice, and what does the floor trade off?
rubric: The retail PD floor lives in CRR Art.163(1); Art.160(1) governs corporate/institution exposures — citing Art.160 for a retail-pooled PD is a real error.
The floor value (~0.03%) is a regulatory value, not an ÖRS modelling choice; it is a live figure under CRR III.
The tradeoff: it surrenders risk-sensitivity (your best grades cannot earn a sub-floor PD even if your data supports it) for a hard backstop against optimistic tails collapsing capital toward zero.

cards.front: The Leitfaden reuses a fixed 45% LGD instead of estimating it. Senior management asks: is the 45% a regulatory value or an ÖRS modelling decision? Resolve and produce the tradeoff.

tags.risk: reg constant vs ÖRS proportionality reuse

rubric: The 45% senior-unsecured LGD is itself a CRR Foundation-IRB regulatory value (reg).
Reusing that constant inside the Leitfaden — rather than self-estimating LGD — is an ÖRS proportionality decision (ors), a consequence of the regime the primaries already inhabit.
The tradeoff: simplicity and regulatory alignment versus surrendered risk-sensitivity — a heavily-secured mortgage book is genuinely over-capitalised at 45%.
Capturing that collateral benefit would require migrating to A-IRB with the full estimation, validation and downturn-LGD machinery; the sector judges that not worth it for most primaries.

cards.front: Explain to the Aufsichtsrat why the LGD entering the Vasicek formula must be a downturn LGD that exceeds the long-run average.

rubric.text: The Vasicek formula stresses PD to the 99.9th percentile of the systematic factor, but LGD enters as a multiplicative constant — it is NOT stressed by the formula.
LGD and PD are positively correlated through the cycle: in a downturn more borrowers default AND collateral values fall, so recoveries shrink exactly when defaults spike.
A long-run-average LGD plugged into a downturn-PD formula therefore understates capital, because it assumes recoveries are as good in the crash as on average.
EBA/GL/2019/03 fix: feed a downturn-calibrated LGD; if no material downturn effect is evidenced, apply an add-on / minimum margin as a fallback.

antiPoints: Claiming the Vasicek formula already stresses LGD to 99.9%.
Claiming LGD and PD are independent / uncorrelated through the cycle.
cards.modelAnswer: The supervisory formula pushes PD to the 99.9% systematic-factor tail but takes LGD as a flat multiplicative constant, so it never stresses recoveries itself. Empirically LGD and PD move together — in a downturn defaults spike while collateral values collapse, so recoveries are worst precisely when defaults are highest. Plugging a long-run-average LGD into that stressed-PD formula therefore understates capital, which is why EBA/GL/2019/03 requires a downturn-calibrated LGD (≥ the long-run average), with an add-on as a fallback where no material downturn effect can be evidenced.

cards.front: Defend your Margin of Conservatism to a TRIM-style on-site inspection: decompose it and avoid the two classic failures.

rubric.text: Final estimate = best estimate + MoC, decomposed into A (data/methodological deficiencies), B (relevant changes to underwriting/collection/risk appetite), C (general/residual statistical estimation error).
Category C must capture ONLY residual statistical uncertainty and must not re-capture the deficiencies already quantified in A or the change effects in B (no double-count).
The MoC is separate from the Art.181(1)(b) appropriate adjustment and is not a substitute for fixing the data; each component is traced to a specific identified deficiency/change/quantified error.
The MoC is applied at the level of the final estimate, not buried in intermediate steps.

antiPoints: Describing the MoC as a slush fund tuned until capital looks comfortable.
Using the MoC as a substitute for fixing the data or for the Art.181(1)(b) appropriate adjustment.
cards.modelAnswer: I present the regulatory parameter as best estimate plus a categorised MoC: Category A for data and methodological deficiencies, B for relevant changes in underwriting, collection or risk appetite, and C for the residual statistical estimation error of the point estimate. Each component is traced to a specific, documented deficiency, change or quantified confidence interval, and Category C is scoped to exclude anything already counted in A or B so there is no double-count. The MoC is applied at the level of the final estimate and is kept distinct from the Art.181(1)(b) appropriate adjustment, which separately corrects a structural gap in the long-run average — it is neither a slush fund nor a substitute for repairing the underlying data.

cards.front: A junior analyst, 'being conservative', adds a positive margin to every LGD input — including the cure rate. What is wrong, and what is the governing principle?

rubric.text: Conservatism is defined by direction: an adjustment is prudent only if it INCREASES the final capital number.
A higher cure rate means more defaults are assumed to recover without loss, which LOWERS pool LGD and capital — so a positive add-on to the cure rate is anti-conservative (wrong sign).
Prudence on the cure rate means assuming FEWER cures (a lower cure rate raises LGD); the same direction-discipline applies to the Art.181(1)(b) appropriate adjustment.
For PD and LGD themselves the conservative direction is upward.

antiPoints: Claiming adding a margin to every input is always prudent.
Claiming the cure rate does not affect LGD.
cards.modelAnswer: Conservatism is not 'add a positive number everywhere' — it is 'move the final capital number up'. The cure rate enters LGD inversely: \(\text{LGD}=(1-\pi_{\text{cure}})\text{LGD}_{\text{loss}}+\pi_{\text{cure}}\text{LGD}_{\text{cure}}\), so raising the cure rate lowers pool LGD and reduces capital, making a positive margin on it anti-conservative. The prudent move is to assume fewer cures, and the analyst must check the sign of every adjustment — including the Art.181(1)(b) appropriate adjustment — against whether it actually increases the capital outcome.
